question: Will the UK increase the qualifying period for settlement to 10 years before May 2026?
summary: Official policy signals indicate a 10-year baseline under earned settlement, with rollout anticipated in 2026.
Final adoption hinges on the February 2026 consultation results and parliamentary approval, creating timing risk.
Current official guidance still describes a 5-year ILR path for most routes, signaling uncertainty about immediate change.
Political and fairness concerns could lead to delays or more targeted transitional arrangements.

justification.critique_assessment: Objections are valid and point to real risks of delay and non-finalization, though not evidence against the general direction.
justification.adjustment: Adjusted probability downward from 0.92 to 0.87 to reflect timing risk and current guidance incongruence; still a high-likelihood outcome given official signals.

forecasts.reference-class: Earned settlement baseline: proposed policy to raise the standard qualifying period for settlement to 10 years (with potential reductions based on contributions) under UK immigration reform,ется with implementation anticipated from April 2026 (subject to consultation).

sources.claim: The default qualifying period for settlement will be increased from 5 years to 10 years, with a time-adjustment model based on four pillars (Character, Integration, Contribution, Residence) and a 12-week consultation.

The May 2025 immigration white paper proposed increasing the standard qualifying period from five to ten years (with some cases qualifying sooner), and changes to permanent residence rules are planned to begin in April 2026, though final decisions depend on the consultation (which closed in February 2026).
Immigration white paper proposes automatic settlement after 10 years instead of five, with uncertainty about retroactivity to those already in the UK.
Consultation proposes moving from automatic to earned settlement and extending the baseline qualifying period to 10 years, with potential reductions, and could be implemented as early as April 2026.
A letter notes government plans to double the ILR waiting period to 10 years and mentions a consultation running through February 12, 2026.

Current guidance shows the Skilled Worker route still has a 5-year qualifying period for settlement, with long residence requiring 10 years; no final extension to 10 years is reflected in the 2025 guidance.
Long residence is a 10-year route to settlement, illustrating a separate 10-year path but not a blanket extension of the 5-year ILR route for all categories.
GOV.UK announces earned settlement concept; default 10-year qualifying period; four pillars; consultation; rollout planned from April 2026.
EIN reports Home Office consultation proposing to double ILR qualifying period from 5 to 10 years, with higher period for lower-skilled workers.
Guardian reports government proposes extending settlement wait to 10 years; consultation ongoing as part of white paper.
Migration Observatory analysis explaining changes to settlement include 10-year baseline with potential reductions for integration and contributions.
Financial Times reports the government preparing a major overhaul to settlement rules—10-year baseline with potential exemptions; implementation likely around 2026.

causal-factors.name: Official consultation favors earned settlement with 10-year baseline
causal-factors.rationale: Multiple official documents and reputable outlets indicate the policy proposal to raise the standard qualifying period to 10 years with earned settlement, increasing the expected probability of adoption.

causal-factors.name: Planned implementation aligned to April 2026
causal-factors.rationale: Implementation signaling for April 2026 raises the likelihood that the change could be in effect before May 2026 if final decisions are made.

causal-factors.name: Parliamentary and policy hurdles / fairness concerns (retroactivity)
causal-factors.rationale: Debates about retroactivity and fairness could delay or soften the policy, dampening the probability.

causal-factors.name: Current guidance maintains a 5-year ILR path; policy not yet finalized
causal-factors.rationale: Existing official guidance still shows a 5-year path; until final decisions are made, the change remains uncertain.

causal-factors.name: Earned settlement baseline raised to 10 years (policy proposal)
causal-factors.rationale: The government explicitly proposes moving the baseline to 10 years as part of the earned settlement model and has launched a 12-week consultation to shape the details. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/earned-settlement/a-fairer-pathway-to-settlement-statement-and-accompanying-consultation-on-earned-settlement-accessible))

causal-factors.name: Implementation timeline signals (April 2026 rollout)
causal-factors.rationale: Commons Library notes changes to permanent residence are planned to begin in April 2026, with the earned settlement consultation having closed by February 2026, moving toward enactment. ([commonslibrary.parliament.uk](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-10267/))

causal-factors.name: Public/fairness backlash risk (retroactivity concerns)
causal-factors.rationale: Analyses and media coverage warn about large numbers potentially affected (including children), and concerns about retroactivity and fairness could slow or dilute the policy. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/feb/09/children-settled-status-home-office-plans-ippr?utm_source=openai))

causal-factors.name: Guidance lag and incomplete policy bake-in (5-year ILR still in guidance)
causal-factors.rationale: Current continuous residence guidance still describes a 5-year qualifying period for most routes, indicating the 10-year reform has not yet fully replaced operational rules. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/continuous-residence/continuous-residence-guidance-accessible-version?utm_source=openai))

causal-factors.name: Time-adjustment reductions for contributions (potential early settlement for high earners/contributors)
causal-factors.rationale: The earned settlement framework envisages reductions from 10 years based on pillars like English proficiency, earnings, public service, volunteering, creating room for earlier settlement for some. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/earned-settlement/a-fairer-pathway-to-settlement-statement-and-accompanying-consultation-on-earned-settlement-accessible))

causal-factors.name: Group-specific longer waits (e.g., 15 years for low/mid-skilled care workers; 20 years for refugees)
causal-factors.rationale: Migration Observatory analysis shows some cohorts face much longer baseline waits, signaling implementation challenges and political pushback. ([migrationobservatory.ox.ac.uk](https://migrationobservatory.ox.ac.uk/resources/commentaries/changes-to-settlement-what-do-they-mean/?utm_source=openai))

causal-factors.name: Transitional arrangements and parliamentary oversight (transitions for those already here)
causal-factors.rationale: The process contemplates transitional provisions to ease impact and ongoing parliamentary scrutiny, which could support smoother adoption. ([commonslibrary.parliament.uk](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-10267/))

causal-factors.name: Official policy direction: earned settlement with 10-year baseline
causal-factors.rationale: GOV.UK consultations and white papers explicitly outline a 10-year baseline and earned settlement framework, signaling a clear policy shift.

causal-factors.name: Implementation timeline: phased rollout starting April 2026
causal-factors.rationale: Multiple sources indicate the rollout could begin in April 2026, increasing the likelihood that the 10-year path takes effect before May 2026.

causal-factors.name: Transitional and retrospective considerations
causal-factors.rationale: Uncertainty around retroactivity and transitional protections could slow adoption or alter the final design.

causal-factors.name: Policy debate and fairness concerns among stakeholders
causal-factors.rationale: Public and political debate on fairness and potential retroactive effects may delay final decisions or lead to concessions.

synthesis: The ensemble points to a high chance of a 10-year ILR threshold by May 2026, but credible objections about finalization and political hurdles justify a modest downward adjustment from the raw ensemble probability.
